rv.q: This cause celebre of a show turns out to be a joyous, funny, and sweet production that should appeal to several generations of musical fans.
The Prom is a big, bright, fizzy musical that tackles LGBTQ issues with heart, humor and a killer cast of Broadway veterans who know exactly how to sell a song.
With its kinetic dancing, broad mugging and belty anthems, it makes you believe in musical comedy again.
It’s big silly fun, with a sly wink and a warm heart.
Joyously affectionate...It's heartening to see a second musical about the lesbian experience on Broadway.

Joined by a puffed-up actor-waiter (Christopher Sieber) and a leggy career chorus girl (Angie Schworer, who looks like someone stretched Jane Krakowski on a rack), Dee Dee and Barry decamp—albeit very campily—to rural Indiana.
That's 'The Prom,' a savvy, self-aware, self-serving and consistently funny new musical of liberal longing.

Indeed, it's hard to imagine a show fueled by more extravagant good will than Prom, which Nicholaw put together with old friends and collaborators Chad Beguelin, Bob Martin and Matthew Sklar, with Martin and Beguelin co-writing the book and the latter crafting lyrics for Sklar's music.
The Prom undeniably is entertaining, but as a lyric in a Forbidden Broadway might describe this frisky though significantly misguided musical: The Prom is a bomb with aplomb.

Many important social issues — inclusion, arts education, community outreach — get run over by lame humor, underwhelming songs and ultra-hammy performances in this original musical, which is so flimsy, tacky and amateurish that it leaves you wondering how it got to Broadway in the first place.
The Prom thrives by going beyond “enough.”

In this current political climate, that is experiencing a monumental moral schism, it might be said that this is not a Broadway musical for everyone and that it may offend a certain audience.
“The Prom” is hysterically funny, with a real sense of joy, Nicholaw-directed dances, and all the stuff that has made shows like “Aladdin,” “Spamalot,” and even “Mean Girls” so winning.
Ineptitude, inflated egos and teenage angst will likely never be this much fun.

Like it’s well-meaning characters, THE PROM doesn’t intend to demean or condescend but it does both.

The first scenes of The Prom, a new Broadway musical comedy that makes gleeful fun of Broadway performers, are as deliriously funny as any musical of recent vintage. Of course, satirizing the world of Broadway is right in the wheelhouse of the show's co-creator Bob Martin, the Canadian Tony-winning librettist best known for The Drowsy Chaperone.
A well-intentioned new musical that is poorly executed.

Definitely a fun night out at the theater going to a prom unlike one you’ve ever attended!

cn.t: Critics find "The Prom" a joyful, big-hearted musical comedy with standout performances, particularly from Beth Leavel and Brooks Ashmanskas, though some fault its formulaic plot and heavy-handed messaging. Most praise its infectious energy and Broadway self-satire.

sg.ra: Longacre's proscenium is narrow (35ft wide, 34'10" high) and the house is shallow, so Row D sits very close without neck-craning; Center Orchestra rows D-L fall inside the mezzanine overhang line (which starts around Row H) but the overhang is shallow enough that top-of-stage cut-off is not reported here, unlike deeper houses.

Longacre is a small-to-mid house (1,077 seats) so 'rear' orchestra is still close by Broadway standards; rows L-N sit behind the mezzanine overhang line (starts ~H) which trims a small slice of upper stage but preserves intimacy and drops the price noticeably versus premium D-K.

Longacre's mezzanine is 'not too high' per SeatPlan - the overhang from the balcony only starts at Row B, so Row A gets a clean head-on elevated view, and unusually generous front-row legroom is a Longacre-specific quirk called out on BroadwayWorld.

Rows D-E sit under the balcony overhang (starts Row B) but Longacre's balcony is small (249 seats, 7 rows) so the overhang depth is modest; sources consistently flag D-E as the honest middle-ground for elevated sightlines before rows F-J start feeling far from the stage.

Longacre's mezzanine rake flattens toward the back per SeatPlan ('the rake may also be slightly too shallow if a taller patron is sitting in front'), and rows F-J are explicitly called out as 'problematic' and 'not the best on account of their considerable distance from the stage' - the small house becomes a disadvantage here since the balcony takes over the better upper-level views.

Longacre-specific quirk: the front balcony rail sits high enough that multiple TripAdvisor reviewers at 5'5" and 5'7" had to lean over the bar the whole show (Macbeth 2022, Swept Away-era 2025), so Row B beats Row A for most patrons - the opposite of the usual 'front row is always best' advice. Also avoid the four structural pillars between rows B and C on the center aisles.

sg.vl: Skip for any show with detail
sg.ra: Longacre's balcony is the oldest-school part of the house - a 1913 Henry B. Herts design with four structural pillars between B-C and a steep rake that gets sound-dead at the back; SeatPlan explicitly warns 'sound quality may be inferior toward the rear' and rows D-G compound distance + pillar risk + tight legroom.
